As I understand it, 7.1 sound is what you are thinking of.

center, front right, front left, Sub, rear center, side fill right side fill left. Both sides can be mounted above, behind your head. The sphere of sound is done using timing tricks with the rear channels.
I bet that upstairs and downstairs neighbors would have different opinions on that.

Funny thing about that, we're actually very bad at identifying the vertical location of sound sources. We can do it somewhat with front and back, but our abilities to detect the elevation of a sound by hearing alone are pretty limited except in some specific cases.

You think you recognize sound sources as being above you, but it's much more likely that you're relying on prior knowledge - for instance, if I hear a helicopter, I know that's an 'up' sound. I look for it in the sky, but not because I can hear it's above me, I'm relying on lateral (left/right) localization, and then looking up due to prior knowledge. But if you were to somehow magically be suspended in mid-air, with your eyes closed, a helicopter flying under you would sound nearly identical to a helicopter flying over you (if you held your head still and level, at least, like you do when you watch a movie).

That's why this 'sphere' of sound hasn't caught on, even though people have experimented with it. Stereo made a big difference over mono, because we hear left/right very well. Surround sound didn't make as big of a difference as stereo, but was still an advance, because we do pretty good with front/back (the ridges in our ears filter sound, and we subconsciously learn to recognize the sound of something being filtered by the back of our ear as opposed to the front of our ear). But with up/down, it's such a small range of sound that we can effectively localize that it's not generally a noticeable difference.
Dolby atmos does this. For 7.1 systems it the back left and right channels can be swapped with the front ceiling reflective speakers.
